verses.1: Al-Mizan defines tasbīḥ as exalting God above every deficiency, need, and imperfect quality, and says that whatever is in heaven and earth—rational and non-rational beings alike—performs it. This is not merely the figurative testimony of creatures’ existence or their state, nor solely rational beings’ verbal speech: (17:44) shows that all things glorify Him in speech which humans do not understand, as (41:21) says all things are given speech. God is al-ʿAzīz, overcoming all without being overcome, and al-Ḥakīm, whose perfect acts cannot be undone or objected to.
verses.2: Al-Mizan says the exclusive kingdom of heaven and earth belongs to God because all things originate from and subsist through Him; no other rule, sovereignty, or authority exists. His giving life and bringing death are continuous and all-encompassing: they include angels’ life, fetal life, Resurrection, inanimate things’ death, worldly death, and the second death in Barzakh (40:11). The closing assertion of power over everything especially removes the thought that He could not restore one whose remains have vanished.
verses.3: Al-Mizan makes God absolutely the First before every supposed first, the Last after every supposed last, more Manifest than every manifest thing, and more Hidden beyond every hidden thing, because His power encompasses all things from every angle. These attributes are neither temporal nor spatial; all other instances of them are relative. They follow from His all-encompassing power, existence, and knowledge: He precedes origination and remains after annihilation, is nearer than all manifest things, and lies beyond minds and imaginations. The readings that make Him first without beginning, last without end, manifest as all-triumphant, or hidden beyond sense express related meanings, while other interpretations are omitted as valueless.
verses.4: Al-Mizan treats God’s settling on the Throne as a metaphor for governing His dominion, followed by knowledge of every particular as governance requires. He knows rainwater and seeds entering earth, plants, animals, and springs emerging, water, sunlight, and angels descending, and vapors, angels, and servants’ deeds ascending. His being with people wherever they are means they are never absent from His encompassing presence across place, time, or state, though some explain it as the reach of His knowledge. Consequently He sees not only deeds’ outward form but their inward intentions and aims.
verses.5: Al-Mizan says the repeated kingdom of heaven and earth shows that all things return to God because they ultimately belong to Him, whereas the earlier occurrence showed that they originate with Him. The definite plural al-umūr makes the return universal: all command and authority are His. Replacing a pronoun with the name Allah here and in the preceding verse gives the statement a deeper effect on listeners, a device repeated in the chapter’s Resurrection and spending passages.
verses.6: Al-Mizan explains God’s making night enter day and day enter night as the seasonal variation of their lengths, with one increasing in the northern hemisphere as it decreases in the southern. His knowledge of what is in breasts reaches hidden thoughts and intentions, including those of the heart, and completes the preceding assertion that He sees the outward form of deeds.
verses.7: Al-Mizan addresses believers and reads the command to faith as a demand that existing faith be confirmed and raised through action. Spending in God’s way is faith’s practical effect, while refusal to spend betrays a deficiency in it. God made them mustakhlafīn either as His vicegerents entrusted with wealth or as inheritors of earlier generations’ wealth; both readings make parting with it easier, since it belongs to God and cannot remain with them. Belief and spending bring the promised great reward.
verses.8: Al-Mizan again understands faith as faith visibly realized in action, including spending. The Messenger calls them to believe because God is their Lord and they are obliged to obey Him. The covenant is most fittingly the commitment to God’s oneness and the Messenger’s truth made when they believed, which entails hearing and obedience; it may belong to God or the Messenger. The proposed pre-world covenant in ʿālam al-dharr is rejected because the audience does not know it and it embraced all humans, not believers alone.
verses.9: Al-Mizan identifies the manifest signs as Qur’anic verses that clarify religious obligations and bring people from the darkness of unbelief to the light of faith. The agent of this bringing forth may be God or His Messenger, with the same ultimate significance because faith in the Messenger is faith in God. God’s kindness and mercy show that the faith and spending to which they are called benefit the believers, not God or His Messenger.
verses.10: Al-Mizan says God’s heritage encompasses all owned things in heaven and earth: human ownership is a social arrangement that death continually transfers between generations until only God remains. This heritage belongs to Him both because He grants temporary ownership and because He survives every possessor; the second sense is most fitting here. The verse strongly rebukes withholding wealth that will not remain with anyone. Spending and fighting before the victory—whether the conquest of Mecca or Ḥudaybiyya—rank higher, and the context makes the spending expenditure for jihād, yet God promises the best reward also to those who spent and fought later, so they need not despair. His awareness confirms the entire judgment.
verses.11: Al-Mizan defines qard as wealth given to be returned, originally a portion detached from its owner, and yuḍāʿif as multiplication manyfold. Calling expenditure a good loan to God is a powerful inducement: God repays not merely its capital but many times over and adds ajr karīm, an unfailingly pleasing Hereafter reward. Yet all action and capacity belong rightfully to God; the servant alone benefits from the reward, which is pure divine grace rather than something earned from God. Ajr is beneficial reward, unlike jazāʾ, which may be beneficial or harmful.
verses.12: Al-Mizan makes the promised noble reward the Day of Judgment, when believing men and women of every prophetic nation move by light before them and on their right, the side of felicity. Its movement shows their progress through increasingly illuminated degrees of Paradise and nearness until their light is complete ((39:73); (19:85); (66:8)). Angels, by God’s command, announce their everlasting gardens; ‘the great success’ may be God’s statement referring to their light and good news, or the angels’ statement referring to the gardens and abiding there.
verses.13: Al-Mizan says hypocrites remain outwardly among believers at the beginning of the Hereafter but are swallowed by darkness while the faithful hasten by their light. They ask the faithful to wait so they can borrow light. ‘Go back and grope for light’ may mock their worldly mockery, or expose the impossibility of returning to the world to acquire faith and righteous deeds; it may instead send them to the place where light was apportioned, where they find none and return to a barrier. The wall with a gate separates faithful from hypocrites, perhaps the Heights, and mirrors their worldly association behind a spiritual veil. Mercy lies inside with the sincere and punishment outside with hypocrites; the gate lets them glimpse Paradise, worsening grief and regret.
verses.14: Al-Mizan says the hypocrites appeal to their former outward companionship with believers, who answer that this was true only externally. They had put themselves to trial and perished, awaited the religion’s defeat, doubted it, were deceived by hopes of its extinction, and finally by Satan until death arrived. These are diseases of their hearts, unlike the sound heart alone that benefits on the Day when wealth and children do not (26:89).
verses.15: Al-Mizan says the faithful tell hypocrites and open disbelievers that no ransom can release anyone held by worldly deeds. Fire is their exclusive mawlā, mockingly called their ally or refuge, so no helper can save them. Mawlā may also mean the affair’s ultimate outcome: because they sought needs from other than God, their final provider is Hell, with Zaqqūm, boiling water, flaming garments, Hell as dwelling, and devils as companions.
verses.16: Al-Mizan understands God’s remembrance as whatever recalls Him and the descended truth as the Qur’an, though both may be the Qur’an, each naturally producing humility. The verse rebukes believers whose hearts have hardened and warns them not to become like earlier People of the Book: as time with an envisaged end, amad, lengthened over them, their hearts hardened and many became transgressors. A hardened heart is untouched by truth and humility and may abandon servanthood for sin.
verses.17: Al-Mizan gives God’s revival of dead earth as a similitude after rebuking hard-hearted believers: it renews their resolve toward humility. It may also announce that God will not leave religion to hardened hearts but replaces them with living hearts that worship as He wills, as in (47:38). The clear signs are given so people apply reason.
verses.18: Al-Mizan says the repeated promise of multiplied return and noble reward intensifies encouragement to spend. It joins charitable men and women to those who lend God a good loan: both charitable giving and expenditure in His way are multiplied and receive the noble reward.
verses.19: Al-Mizan addresses Muslims and People of the Book together by saying faith in God and His messengers, unlike the chapter’s singular ‘Messenger’ when it addresses the Prophet’s community. This is pure faith inseparable from submission and obedience. Such believers are admitted to the rank and reward of the truthful, whose word and deed accord, and the witnesses to deeds on Resurrection—not martyrs—with the same reward and light, rather than necessarily being those ranks in actuality. The alternate parsing that makes martyrs a new sentence is not favored. Disbelievers who deny signs abide in Hell, while the contrast is meant to arouse hope and fear in sinful believers between the saved and perished.
verses.20: Al-Mizan calls worldly life play with imaginary aims, diversion from true ends, adornment, mutual boasting in lineage or rank, and competition for wealth and children. It offers Shaykh Bahāʾī’s report that these traits correspond to life’s stages from childhood play to old-age accumulation. Like rain that delights farmers, vegetation reaches fullness, yellows, and becomes chaff, worldly gains neither endure nor nurture the soul. The Hereafter instead offers severe punishment or God’s forgiveness and pleasure; forgiveness precedes pleasure because it purifies its recipient, and its attribution to God suggests His desire to forgive rather than punish. The world is wares of delusion for whoever is deceived by it.
verses.21: Al-Mizan distinguishes musābaqa, racing to surpass rivals, from merely hurrying, and makes the command to take the lead toward forgiveness and Paradise more demanding than (3:133). It rejects the view that the two verses address different ranks or different-sized paradises: the definite singular al-samāʾ denotes the category of heavens, like the plural. Forgiveness comes first because Paradise’s pure realm requires cleansing from sin; its ʿaraḍ signifies supreme expanse, not a basis for speculative claims about its dimensions. Faith in God and messengers is the lofty faith displayed in righteous deeds and avoidance of transgression, not bare belief that would make the command meaningless for believers. Paradise and forgiveness are grace God wills for such believers, and His grace is immense.
verses.22: Al-Mizan defines muṣība as a misfortune, normally adversity, striking earth through drought, blight, or earthquake and people through illness, injury, or death. Before God brings it from nothingness, it is in the Tablet recording all that was, is, and will be; reducing this to a finite material tablet or replacing it with bare divine knowledge is rejected, except as knowledge at the level of divine acts. Predetermining and irrevocably decreeing events is easy for God. This knowledge should prevent excessive grief over what escapes and exultation over what He gives: losses belong to things’ perishing nature, whereas their existence and continuance are from God. It removes the conceit and boasting that falsely claim personal entitlement to His gifts.

verses.24: Al-Mizan identifies the swaggering braggart as one whose pride in wealth makes him stingy and urges others to be stingy, lest their generosity expose him. Whoever turns from spending and from these admonitions should know that God is al-Ghanī, needing none of their wealth, and al-Ḥamīd in all He does. Together with (57:22) and (57:24), this counsels zuhd: because affairs are decreed before they occur, people should neither grieve over lost wealth nor exult in gain, and should spend rather than hoard.
verses.25: Al-Mizan begins a new account of the religion of truth: messengers came with miracles, prophecy, and decisive arguments; the Book means written revelation—the scriptures of Noah, Abraham, Torah, Evangel, and Qur’an. The Balance may be the ordinary scale enabling just exchange, or more fittingly in context the religion measuring beliefs and deeds; justice or intellect are also proposed. Iron is ‘sent down’ in the Qur’anic sense of creation descending from the Unseen in known measure, and supplies weapons and armor for defense as well as universal human uses. It tests and externally distinguishes those who help God and His messengers through jihād to defend the faithful and spread truth; God needs no helper, being all-strong and all-mighty.
verses.26: Al-Mizan says the descendants of Noah and Abraham received continuing prophethood and scripture. Across their nations until the present, some are guided but many remain transgressors.
verses.27: Al-Mizan says the succession of messengers after Noah and Abraham forms one continuous path, with every later prophet descending from Noah and Jesus also descending from Abraham. Jesus received the Evangel, and his followers were given mutual kindness and mercy, whether by inspiration or command and promised reward. Monasticism, derived from fear, was their own innovation, not God’s prescription; they imposed it seeking His pleasure but failed to observe it properly, while its pursuit of divine pleasure indicates it was still pleasing to Him. Faithful Christians receive their reward, but many are transgressors.
verses.28: Al-Mizan takes the command to believers to have faith in the Messenger as the higher faith of fully following and obeying him in law and rule, not bare belief. It therefore promises reward upon reward: a double mercy, light by which to walk, and forgiveness. The light may be in this world as in (6:122) as well as in the Hereafter, so it should not be restricted to the Resurrection light. The alternative reading makes the double mercy the double reward of believing People of the Book. The following verse most fittingly explains that this promise prevents the People of the Book from supposing the believers lack access to divine grace; the contorted reading with a superfluous li and the pronoun referring to them is rejected. All grace is in God’s hand, granted as He wills.
